entries.title: ‘The Best Thing That Happened to Him Was Losing in 2020’
entries.summary: Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan explain how the four years between Donald Trump’s first and second terms changed the presidency.
entries.content:
Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan explain how the four years between Donald Trump’s first and second terms changed the presidency.

Few reporters understand as much about Donald Trump’s thinking, motives, and behavior as Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan. Haberman has been covering the president closely for more than a decade at The New York Times; she started with his first campaign in 2015, and her record of scoops quickly brought her into the public eye. Swan was, for many years, her chief professional rival: He worked for Axios, where he landed a controversial 2018 one-on-one interview with Trump. In late 2022, the Times announced that it was hiring Swan, turning the rivals into colleagues.

This past June, they published Regime Change: Inside the Imperial Presidency of Donald Trump. The book, an instant best seller, advances a new understanding of the first year of Trump’s second term, relaying in minute-by-minute detail how, since retaking office, he has pursued his personal goals with few limits on his power. The Atlantic staff writer Tim Alberta sat down with both authors at The Atlantic Festival, where he asked them about the 2028 election and the future of the presidency and the Republican Party.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Tim Alberta: Maggie, this country has been through a lot, and I’m wondering if you could help us understand how a “regime change” of this sort came to be.

Maggie Haberman: Essentially, we have had a series of national traumas since 9/11: two forever wars, a fiscal crisis, immense populist anger that started rising in 2010. To me, that was the year that set the tone. It was also the year that the proto-Trump, Carl Paladino, was the Republican nominee for governor in New York State. One of the issues that he ran on was the planned mosque to be built near the World Trade Center; it became known incorrectly as the “Ground Zero Mosque,” and it became a clear avatar of a change in this country after the era of George W. Bush. So you get to 2014, when immigration and particularly border crossings were on the rise under President Obama. Suddenly, this became a massive issue within the Republican Party. You had this mix of anger over the wars, anger over the massive accumulated debt under President Bush, then Obamacare, anger about immigration, and a shifting job market. The time was ripe for a candidate who presented himself as a fighter—and who was already known to most of the Republican electorate, not just as a celebrity on The Apprentice but as a cultural figure.

Alberta: 2016, Trump 1.0, is its own story. So much of what this book is about is how the end of that first term, and then his time in exile after losing in 2020, shapes this dramatic, radical, wholesale change to government and to executive power.

Jonathan Swan: When we were reporting for this book, we heard from a couple of people who were close to Trump at a pretty high level that, in their view, the best thing that happened to him was losing in 2020. Which is something they could never say publicly or in his presence, because, of course, he never lost the election and what have you. But it’s indisputably true. Let’s say Trump ekes out that victory in 2020: He comes back in; he is hobbled by COVID. He has the same inflation that every other country around the world has. He still has the rump of a team around him that he really doesn’t like very much, who are, in quite a few instances, pushing back on some of his more extreme desires. He really can’t get his arms around the presidency.

Instead, he loses. People like Stephen Miller spent those four years very productively. It wasn’t just drawing up the plans—you saw that blitz of executive orders at the start of 2025, which was all very well prepared. They also spent a lot of time thinking about Who are the lawyers that we want to fill the government with? And I’m not just talking about the White House counsel’s office; I’m talking about across the government. Agency lawyers, general counsels—they would constantly say, Well, no, what you’re proposing is illegal. But when you have lawyers who are saying, Well, actually, if we turn it this way and then turn it this way and then give it a little bit of a spin, then they can bless what you want. And that’s what’s happening.

I’ll give you the perfect example that describes the difference between term one and term two: In term one, Trump was saying almost yearningly, You know, they don’t have a drug problem in China, because Xi Jinping, he just kills the drug dealers. And they don’t have a drug problem in the Philippines, because Rodrigo Duterte just kills them. Trump was very fond of these extrajudicial killings. In term one, there wasn’t a huge amount of enthusiasm for this idea among the leadership of the Defense Department. Now you have Pete Hegseth, and you have lawyers inside the government that allow a policy where Donald Trump decided, in his mind, that people on fishing boats transporting cocaine in the Caribbean Sea are not drug traffickers who are to be interdicted by the Coast Guard and dealt with in a criminal-justice system. No: They’re enemy combatants in a war. We’re not going to interdict them. We’re not going to arrest them. We’re just going to kill them. And that’s something that has been blessed within the government. They haven’t even bothered to try to legally justify this in a public setting. They just do it, knowing that they have the right lawyers in place.

The other big element making this term unrecognizable from the first term is the immunity decision. Maggie and I talk about this all the time. Trump would say early on, I’m immune; I’m immune. He has said privately that he’s going to pardon anyone who came within 250 feet of the Oval Office.

The point is, he had the time to rebuild, and his team had time to prepare. That’s how you get this second term.

Alberta: Trump can’t stay in power forever. He will soon be a lame duck after these November midterms. I’m wondering how he’s handling that: whether he is going to allow a neat and tidy process to unfold for his successor, and whether or not J. D. Vance, who got a bit crosswise with him over Iran, is going to be tortured over the next several years as the president deliberates over whom he should hand all of this over to.

Swan: We have a scene in the book that I think illustrates what you’re describing. Rupert Murdoch comes to the White House for dinner. This is October of last year, and they’re in the Blue Room of the White House. And at the table are J. D. Vance and Marco Rubio.

Haberman: And, like, 10 other people.

Swan: Halfway through the conversation, Trump says, I really like J.D. I really like Marco. Rupert, what do you think of J.D.? And he starts this beauty pageant, essentially, in front of both of them, with the most powerful proprietor of conservative media—knowing full well that Rupert Murdoch is no fan of J. D. Vance and, in fact, tried to stop him from becoming the vice president. There’s this pause, and Rupert Murdoch says, J.D. has the potential to be great—just withering. Vance says, Oh, gee, thanks, Rupert. It’s a very awkward moment. Trump says, What do you think of Marco? And Rupert doesn’t miss a beat: He says, Marco’s brilliant. This savage moment just foretells what the next two years are going to be like. How is he grappling with being a lame duck? The way he’s grappling with it is by refusing to be a lame duck.

Vance is in a really difficult position because, as you noted, there were several meetings leading up to the Iran war, in the Situation Room and the Oval Office, where Vance was the only one in the room arguing against it. That did not go down well with Trump. And so the notion that this is going to be some smooth glide path to the 2028 nomination is contradicted by every piece of evidence we have about who Donald Trump is and how he behaves.

Alberta: Maggie, that point that Jonathan makes about Trump’s refusal to be a lame duck over the next two years—what does that look like?

Haberman: I don’t want to limit anyone’s imagination here on what it would look like. The question that we get a lot is, Will he try for a third term? I truly don’t believe he will, but I’m absolutely willing to be wrong. I don’t actually think he wants that, and he doesn’t need it. He will be the dominant figure in this party until he is no longer on this Earth, whether he’s in office or not. He has made more money than he ever made in his life during this presidency—at least just liquid, that we know of, assets.

Swan: By orders of magnitude.

Haberman: The crypto money is, I think, $2.2 billion in the first year-ish of the presidency. His children have continued to make money. There were very valid questions about Hunter Biden, but it is so dwarfed by everything that we are seeing now, everything that Hunter Biden was doing.

What the next two years I expect will look like will be the projects Trump really cares about, which are these monuments to himself in Washington—the ballroom. I’m very curious to see what happens with the Kennedy Center; that’s a big open question. This is not going to look like any kind of congressional flip that we’ve seen before in a lame-duck presidency, because to Jonathan’s point, Trump knows that he is immune from federal prosecution. He has talked about pardons very openly. We spoke with a number of people who are counting on their pardons. We’ve never seen a government just not respond to subpoenas in Congress. The only recourse that Congress has if they don’t get cooperation is a contempt-of-Congress vote and a referral to the Department of Justice, where I’m confident Attorney General Todd Blanche is not going to do a lot. This is a government that has done so little in terms of legislating. Everything, for the most part, was by executive action.

Alberta: Your reporting describes a government that is not recognizable at a fundamental level. How do we come back from that?

Haberman: That’s the reason for the title.

Swan: It’s such an interesting question, because on the one hand, there will be a desire by many to restore what was before. On the other hand, Trump has also shown what you can do unilaterally. He’s demonstrated, particularly in the second term, that a lot of the constraints that we take for granted around the presidency are not legal constraints. They’re self-restraint or norms. Just take the ballroom, for example. Yes, in the end, it was green-lighted, right? The court system is not stopping him from building this ballroom. But by the time the court system got up to that point, there was a giant hole in the ground. There were cranes in the sky; there were shovels going through the earth.

The tariffs are another great example: Yes, ultimately, the Supreme Court checked him on his tariffs—months after he started a global trade war, which had all kinds of rippling consequences. This is a legal system that is not built to deal with a president like Donald Trump; he has shown that you can just get away with acting and forcing others to react. That was a deliberate strategy—overwhelm the opposition; overwhelm the legal groups.

So you have two models: One is a figure who comes back and says, Actually, we need to restore checks and balances and the constitutional system. Or you have either a right-wing populist or a left-wing populist saying, You know what? Donald Trump has actually shown us what nirvana could look like if we do it on behalf of our chosen priorities. That’s how you can get potentially even more of an expansion of executive power and the imperial presidency.

Haberman: The one addendum I would make is that I think that for the most part, President Biden did try going back. He really did. He did fairly little by executive action; he had big legislation; he left the Justice Department alone. What I hear from Democrats I speak with is that they want someone who is going to fight in the manner that they have seen Republicans fight. I agree with Jonathan that I don’t think there is another Donald Trump walking around; I think he is sui generis for a lot of reasons. But that doesn’t mean there are not aspects that would be appealing. And certainly, I believe that whoever the next Republican nominee is, they’re going to be in the mold of Donald Trump. I mean, this is Donald Trump’s party until there is another Republican president, not just nominee, or for as long as he is alive. Whatever you see the Democrats form will be a reaction to that.

The only other asterisk is that if ever there was an election cycle that was ripe for a Ross Perot type, it will be 2028. There is so much anger at the system. Part of why Trump is struggling right now in polls is that he broke several campaign promises, and voters can feel that. They can feel $4.50 gas. People want to feel like somebody is actually helping them.

entries.title: When Meditation Has a Dark Side
entries.summary: Could there really be such a thing as too much mindfulness?
entries.content:
Could there really be such a thing as too much mindfulness?

Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts

Twenty years ago, a meditation teacher and doctoral candidate in clinical psychology named Willoughby Britton set out to do a study showing that meditation improves sleep. She divided up the participants, sent them to a sleep lab to monitor their brain activity, and discovered that the results were the opposite of what she had hoped for: The more they meditated, the worse their quality of sleep got. Britton had already experienced benefits of meditation herself, which are well documented in medical literature: It soothes anxiety, chronic pain, and depression, and it lowers blood pressure, alleviates back pain, and has many other benefits, as well.

But as she continued to look into it, Britton kept discovering what seemed, at first, like exceptions: people who actually became more anxious or unmotivated after meditating. Then she began encountering people who experienced more serious mental-health side effects, such as paranoia, hallucinations, and dissociation. Britton became a researcher at Brown University and eventually developed a robust body of work showing that meditation—for certain people and at certain intensities—can be harmful.

On this episode of Radio Atlantic is the staff writer Olga Khazan, who interviewed Britton about her research. We talk about how the meditation community responded, how Britton’s life changed after it was released, and what her recommendations are for the average person interested in meditation.

The following is a transcript of the episode:

Hanna Rosin: Just a quick warning: This episode mentions suicide. If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text the U.S. National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 988.

[Music]

Rosin: This is Radio Atlantic. I’m Hanna Rosin.

I meditate, now and again. Or, at least, I try. I was once at a yoga retreat where early-morning meditation was one of the things on the schedule. I woke up, sat down, and lasted about 12 minutes, which felt like 90.

I downloaded the Calm app a couple of years ago, and I have used it exactly zero times.

I have a doctor friend who assured me that meditation was one of a handful of nonmedicine treatments that had been thoroughly vetted by peer-reviewed science journals, so I never gave up trying. I just assumed that this was my fault and I needed to get better at it.

I have definitely absorbed the idea that there is a meditation ideal to strive towards, a master of serene who manages to both embody a Western principle of high-stress job and an Eastern principle of no stress at all.

Olga Khazan: So I don’t know exactly how it made the leap over from India to America. I think that happened in the 19th century.

Rosin: This is staff writer Olga Khazan.

Khazan: But this modern moment of meditation that we’re living in started in Silicon Valley tech companies. So probably around 10 or 15 years ago, a lot of tech companies—I was gonna say cling, but you’re not really supposed to cling in meditation—they started glomming onto meditation as this solution for people being burned out and overworked. Arianna Huffington got really into it.

Arianna Huffington: There is a deeper dimension to our lives, and we can tap into it.

Khazan: I think Oprah probably did it at one point.

Oprah Winfrey: 9 o’clock in the morning, 4:30 in the afternoon, no matter what’s going on, we stop. We meditate.

Khazan: LeBron James was meditating.

Announcer 1: Look, LeBron meditating there on the bench.

Announcer 2: He’s in that—

Announcer 1: Becoming present.

Announcer 2: He’s in that Calm app.

Announcer 1: Yep.

Khazan: Google had a meditation session for its employees. People in positions of power and authority and people who everyone thought was cool were kind of pushing this idea that meditation is this very benign sort of thing that you can do for yourself in order to make yourself more relaxed.

And I would say that there was a subtext there of, And it’ll make you more productive because you won’t be so obsessed with, like, dumb bullshit. (Laughs.)

[Music]

Rosin: Today, meditation is a multibillion-dollar industry. According to one study, about half of all Americans have tried meditation. And about a fifth do it regularly.

At some point, Olga was one of them. She tried something called MBSR, or mindfulness-based stress reduction, although reluctantly.

Khazan: This was one of the most annoying things about it for me, is that it was very loosey-goosey. But then whenever I asked if I could modify it in some way, it was like, No, that’s the wrong way to do it. (Laughs.)

Rosin: But Olga says it did help relieve some of her anxiety.

Khazan: So even though I wasn’t very good at meditation, I did buy this idea that it’s basically harmless. It seems like, oh, the worst thing that could happen is it just doesn’t work, because you’re not good at it. Honestly, I’ve taken a whole meditation class, where I meditated for 45 minutes a day, and I don’t think anyone ever said, This could be risky.

Rosin: That’s what I always thought, too, and why I at least liked the idea of meditation. It has a low barrier to entry—no fancy, expensive equipment or services required—and seemingly zero side effects.

But then one day, as Olga was browsing online, she came across a researcher at Brown University named Willoughby Britton.

Khazan: So Willoughby Britton started out as a very avid meditator, pretty much as avid as they get.

Willoughby Britton: It was like a lifeline. It was like, I don’t know what I would do without this.

Khazan: So she is a psychologist. She was trained as a psychologist, but as she’s going on her psychology journey, she’s also becoming a really hard-core meditator.

She does other things to kind of show her commitment to this cause. So she’s constantly reading these dharma books, which are books about the Buddhist teachings. She’s teaching meditation through the same meditation class that I took, called MBSR. And she also meditates herself for hours and hours a day.

Britton: I became a meditation teacher. So I had to count my meditation hours, so I know I’m well above 10,000 hours, and I’m probably close to 20,000 hours.

Rosin: Olga ended up talking and meeting up with Willoughby in person. She learned that Willoughby had grown up on a farm in Massachusetts and spent a lot of time by herself as a kid.

Britton: My parents told me that I asked really strange questions like, What is looking out of my eyes? Or, Is today tomorrow? Or things like that. So I was a very curious, weird child.

[Music]

Rosin: Willoughby had always been interested in consciousness and interiority and big existential questions. So in college, she decided to major in neuroscience at Colgate University.

In 1995, during the summer between her junior and senior year, Willoughby’s best friend, Sarah, died by suicide. She’d been overwhelmed by the pressure of being an elite college athlete. According to a New York Times article about her death, Sarah was an “All-Ivy selection in field hockey, ice hockey and lacrosse.” The article states that she was, quote, “found on Monday afternoon by a friend.”

That friend was Willoughby, who found her at her house next to a hunting rifle. After that, Willoughby could not stop thinking about death.

Khazan: I think ultimately, like, what it was is PTSD, is she would think a lot about death and dwell on death and be worried about stepping into an elevator or something ’cause she thought she would find a dead body.

Rosin: So that’s an experience of maybe losing control of your thoughts. It’s a your-brain-is-running-away-from-you kind of feeling.

Khazan: Yeah. So she’s like, I can’t stop thinking about death. So she’s working in labs and stuff ’cause she’s training to be a scientist. And she talks about—they kill the rats after the experiments are over.

Britton: And rats are white with red eyes. And when they die, their eyes turn gold. The blood runs out of them. And so I put them all under a little blanket of paper towels, and I was watching their eyes and being like, Holy shit, this is it. This is the moment that their spirit is departing or whatever.

And so I’m so fascinated by these rats dying, and I asked my colleague, Where does it go? And she was like, Oh, they go in the freezer in 215. And I was like, Okay, I gotta leave. I cannot do this anymore.

Khazan: She’s just getting overly obsessed with death. And she doesn’t wanna take SSRIs. So her father gives her this book called A Path With Heart, by Jack Kornfield. And that book basically is just a very influential meditation book of that time. Kornfield is aiming to bridge the gap between hard-core meditators, who have studied in Tibet and stuff and meditate all the time, and people who are just going through a hard time. So he’s trying to show everyday people how meditation can be helpful to them. And it was really helpful for her. She loved reading the book. She really took it to heart, and that kind of launched her meditation journey.

Rosin: From then on, Willoughby began to devote her life to ancient Buddhist principles. But she also had her degree in neuroscience. So she wanted to use her scientific background to advance the cause of meditation.

Khazan: She does one study in particular that shows that people who meditate more sleep worse.

Britton: They had more fast-wave brain activity. They had more microarousals, awakenings. It was just like every possible metric of cortical arousal was increased.

Khazan: These are not the results she expected. She wanted it to show that people who meditate more sleep better, but they had a worse quality of sleep. They were waking up more, and they spent more time in this phase of sleep that’s associated with restlessness. It really surprised her.

Britton: I was just like, Ah, this is the wrong answer, and maybe I did something wrong. It was the second study I’d ever done. So I was not sure, and I was gonna ruin everything for the field that I was trying to promote. So I just sat on the data.

Khazan: So she shelved that study. She did not publish it. She thought that publishing it would make Buddhism seem bad or make meditation seem bad. So she just was like, Well, maybe this is a one-off. It’s just one study. Who knows? Maybe I did the data wrong or something, and she didn’t publish it.

Rosin: Now, to be clear, meditation has a robust body of research behind it that shows it can improve lots of things: anxiety, chronic pain, depression. There are reputable studies linking it to lower blood pressure, better attention spans, and greater levels of compassion. It can help alleviate back pain, decrease loneliness in older adults, improve memory—which is why Willoughby was so confused by her own results that showed meditation could have any kind of negative effect.

But that was just the first crack.

Khazan: The next thing that happens is that she moves to Rhode Island for her residency. And she’s working at a psychiatric hospital. And she notices that people are coming into the hospital in a state of psychosis, and they’re coming in from meditation retreats.

[Bell tolling]

Khazan: So the first one, she’s like, What’s up with that person? And they’re like, Oh, they’re coming off a meditation retreat. And she’s like, Oh, that’s weird. It can happen. And then the next one, she was like, Wait, what’s up with that person? And they’re like, They’re also coming off a meditation retreat.

Rosin: Wow.

Britton: They were, like, completely psychotic.

Khazan: Wow.

Britton: And so I was like, That’s kind of a lot. That seemed like a lot for one year. Like, here’s my little snapshot of a residency.

Khazan: And so that made her think, Okay, maybe it’s just something about that retreat. And then meditation started to take kind of a dark turn for herself personally.

[Music]

Khazan: What happened to her is that she started experiencing this thing called dissociation. It kind of sounds good at first. And it can be good in really traumatic moments. Dissociating can be a positive thing because it can help you persevere through if your house is on fire and you just need to grab all your stuff and your kids and get out. It’s okay if you’re not totally in the present moment in that time.

Rosin: Yeah.

Khazan: But basically what dissociation involved for her is feeling like she wasn’t really herself, like she was watching a movie of her life and she was a character in it. And this could be really strange feeling. She would feel like her house is not her own.

Britton: It had a feeling of, Oh, I’m in Willoughby’s house, like this other person.

Khazan: If she saw a picture of herself with several friends, she would feel like it was three people she happened to know instead of herself with two other people.

Britton: I thought I was like a camera that was just taking in information. Like, there was no person behind that. And I was like, Oh, my God. How did I forget that? How did I not know that I was actually a person?

Khazan: She had a hard time driving, because she couldn’t figure out where her body began and ended. This is something other people report, is driving can be really tricky when you’re dissociating. And in general, it was very hard to complete a Ph.D. and to launch an academic career when you’re just randomly leaving your body and floating above it in this weird trance state.

Rosin: Dissociation is hard to describe. And when you talk about it, it seems mild, but it’s actually kind of disturbing for the people going through the experience.

Khazan: Yeah. So one person described it to me—not Willoughby—another person described it to me as looking through a veil at your own life and just having all your feelings be really blunted, not being able to enjoy being around your family in the same way, because they don’t feel like they’re your family.

Any time you’ve been on a really bad drug trip—not to expose myself too much, but it can be very unpleasant and, like, What’s happening to me? Is this my brain now? It’s not, like, a cool journey.

Rosin: One theory of why meditation might lead to dissociation is that meditation prompts the prefrontal cortex to essentially shut off. That’s the part of the brain that controls decision making, high-level thinking, and emotions.

And without those emotions to project things onto—how you feel about your body, what you want for lunch, what happened yesterday—you can start to lose a sense of yourself. Hence the dissociation.

Another kind of related theory is that meditation is all about putting yourself in the present. Which can be good, until it’s bad.

Khazan: We map our lives out by what we’re gonna do in the future. So if you think about a toddler dropping something from their high chair, they’re trying to see how they interact with the world and what happens when they do stuff, and that’s how they learn who they are and what they can do in the world and what they should do. It’s a very rudimentary step.

But if you’re never thinking about the future, because you’ve trained your mind to think for hours only about the present moment, your sense of self kind of starts to fall away. You don’t really have a way to root yourself in the narrative of time. You don’t really know who you are anymore.

[Music]

Khazan: Meditation does have a health halo. And something I especially heard from people who went on meditation retreats—which is where you go somewhere else; you stay in a usually very austere, rustic setting; and you meditate pretty much from sunup to sundown, often with a short break where you don’t really talk to other people—people do these in order to relax or recharge.

But it’s really not like a vacation to Cancun. It’s very difficult to force yourself to think about nothing for that long. And if you’re not used to it, in particular, you can kind of start to spiral. And that happened to a lot of the people that I talked to and a lot of the people that Willoughby has interviewed: Their negative experiences started at a retreat.

Rosin: After the break, the dark side of meditation gets a little darker.

[Break]

Rosin: Willoughby Britton had started meditating so much that she was seeing literal stars, which is actually a phenomenon called nimitta in Buddhism.

Britton: N-I-M-I-T-T-A, where when you get really concentrated, you see a light and it looks like, I don’t know, a star or something. But your eyes are open. It’s obvious when your eyes are closed, but it stays there when your eyes are open. So I was having that.

Rosin: Willoughby was also still dissociating—something she was told was a new stage of enlightenment, called “riding the ox backward.” And she was told to keep meditating.

But that only made things worse. So she started interviewing meditation students and teachers about any negative side effects they might’ve experienced too.

Khazan: So some were mild, and some were pretty serious. The most common thing that happened to the people in that sample was fear, anxiety, panic, or paranoia. The second most common thing was changes in motivation, which that can sound like, Okay, that’s fine. You’re not really supposed to be motivated while you’re meditating anyway. But it’s like something where someone just doesn’t wanna do anything.

Britton: So she basically sat on her couch for two years. And she wasn’t depressed. She wasn’t sad. She just couldn’t—there was no impulse to do anything else. If you talked to her, she could speak, but it was like she needed an impulse in order to react, and if there was no input, there would be no output. And she did that for two years.

Khazan: And then there were smaller numbers, but very real people and incidents that happened, which was having delusions, which is a false belief. So that would be, like, I’m the king of the world, or, People are sending me secret messages through street signs, which I think is a real example; hallucinations, so people seeing things that aren’t really there; physical pain, rage, and suicidal ideation, which would be the most serious one. And there have been a few suicides of people who went on meditation retreats and took their own lives not long after that.

One person felt that she needed to save the world from a black-tantric plot contrived by the retreat-center staffers. Someone else began experiencing messianic visions about the need to sacrifice myself in some way for the benefit of saving mankind.

The more disturbing stories that I personally heard from people that I interviewed who had been on meditation retreats involved involuntary movements, so people who couldn’t stop rolling their heads around, for example, or moving their arms or bodies in other ways. And one person actually developed a tic in his face after meditating for a really long time, where half of his face would spasm and stick that way at random and would eventually go back to normal, but he could never really tell when it was gonna happen. That’s the kind of thing that he didn’t have before he started meditating. So something is happening on these retreats that’s prompting people’s brains into this state.

Rosin: Yeah, that’s what I wanted to ask. So these are cases of people who didn’t have these symptoms before. They weren’t diagnosed with, I don’t know, schizophrenia or a propensity to hallucinate or have delusions or anything like that.

Khazan: No. Yeah. So I think with few exceptions, most of the people that I talked to didn’t have the problems that they developed on the meditation retreat beforehand.

Rosin: Right.

Khazan: So they kind of developed new symptoms there. It can happen that it can just exacerbate whatever is already going on with you. But a lot of people did not have experiences of psychosis or other severe problems before they went on retreat. Is it possible that that was just their first manifestation of psychosis in what would become a lifelong bipolar disorder or something like that? I’m not totally sure. It could be. But they didn’t have the diagnosis before they went in.

Rosin: In 2017, after years of interviewing people about the side effects of meditation, Willoughby finally published the findings in a paper called “The Varieties of Contemplative Experience.”

There had been other papers about this topic, but this was the first modern comprehensive study of its kind.

Khazan: It kinda just was, like, the launching point.

Britton: People from all over the world started calling us and were like, Help me. I have a tic, and I can’t work because my tic is so bad. I’m in the hospital. It was just like suddenly I became known for this even though I do a lot of other things.

Khazan: But then she and other people have done further studies showing that this is indeed a thing. So most of the studies settle on a prevalence rate of about 10 percent. So about 10 percent of people who try meditation will have some sort of negative side effect.

Rosin: 10 percent?

Khazan: Yes.

Rosin: Okay.

Khazan: Yeah. And that doesn’t mean that they’ll all be delusional or dissociating. It could just be an increase in anxiety, an increase in depression, something like that where it didn’t help you. It made you feel worse.

Rosin: And did you get the sense that she was just—when you read the research and you evaluated it, did it seem to you like Yeah, she’s just stating the obvious, and there’s been a commercial reason to try and paper it over, or This has been known forever, or These are new things that are associated with meditation in the modern age? Or how did you contextualize it?

Khazan: So I did not know this at all. This was new information to me. But then when I started talking to historians of Buddhism and people who have studied meditation in a more agnostic way, I guess, they said that this is a thing that happens. And even ancient Buddhist texts warn about different—I think they’re called “wind sicknesses” that can happen when you’re meditating and demonic states that you can enter when you’re lost in meditation. And so Buddhists going back into ancient times have also experienced some of these side effects.

And it’s worth noting that in a lot of cultures, we think about it like Anyone can do it, but in a lot of cultures, it wasn’t really common for everyday people to meditate for prolonged stretches at a time. You know, it was a religious practice. And monks did it and people who were trying to reach these new layers of consciousness. It wasn’t something that you do because you had a bad performance review and you wanna get back on your game. And I think that’s part of how this maybe got lost in translation, is that this became something that is a cure-all for everything with no possible externalities. So why not do it as much as possible?

Rosin: Right. Okay. So she has then, with her research—and it sounds like you found it convincing—shifted our notion about meditation, who it’s for, how intensely people should do it. So did that slight modification or reinterpretation of meditation penetrate? Was it received by the meditation community? Did she go out there and preach it, as it were, and change the broader view?

Khazan: Good question. So my—

Rosin: I’m feeling like it’s gonna be a no. I’m feeling like it’s probably no. ’Cause I haven’t heard about it, so I feel like I’m still getting Calm ads for the Calm app, so probably no.

Khazan: So I’ve talked to a lot of other researchers about her research, trying to ask that question. And they run the gamut from I totally reject this. This is BS. No one can hurt themselves meditating—like, one person said her heart hurt that I was working on this story—to Okay, she makes some good points. Maybe schizophrenic people shouldn’t go on meditation retreats, which is what one kind of famous Buddhist scholar told me.

Rosin: So they’re thinking this applies to the outlier of the outlier. It’s not, like, a common variant. It’s just, like, the most outlier case.

Khazan: Yeah, like, if you have some sort of psychological problem, don’t go on a meditation retreat.

Rosin: Uh-huh.

Khazan: So some of them were receptive. Some of her colleagues at Brown spoke with me and said her research is good, she’s courageous, and they’ve incorporated her research into some of the newer meditation classes and the curricula and things like that.

[Music]

Khazan: But she herself felt also very rejected by a lot of people, including her former mentors.

Britton: As the research progressed and even after we published it, there was a lot of backlash. And a lot of the Buddhist teachers that I had practiced under and read their books and sort of worshiped as human beings, they got really nasty.

Khazan: Jack Kornfield, who is the guy who wrote that book that started her meditation journey, gave this quote to a psychology magazine where he said that Willoughby’s work is misleading information and over-the-top fear-mongering. And I think that was really awful for her to hear, because it is a close-knit community. And I think being rejected by someone who’s a father figure and also who set you on your religious journey can just be unusually searing.

Britton: He was, like, an important mentor to me for a while.

Khazan: Yeah, yeah. That’s upsetting.

Britton: Thanks, dad.

Khazan: Thanks, dad, yeah. (Laughs.) That is hard. That’s hard to see.

Khazan: But also, she talks about logistical issues that she started having, like getting funding for some of these studies on the risks of meditation, and the peer-reviewed comments, she would say, were always much longer than her studies about the benefits of meditation. Getting invited to conferences was tough. And when she was invited, she felt like the whole issue of whether meditation had risks was in doubt and she was there to defend this concept.

Britton: Another researcher—I gave a talk at a conference, and he basically started yelling, I don’t believe you. And I was just like, Do you think I’m lying about my data? I have recordings of people saying this. That’s a crazy thing to say to a researcher.

Khazan: So I think there were—she just started to feel a little iced out despite some of the positive reception that she got.

Rosin: And how did you integrate the new information you found out? And I’m using you as a stand-in for me and everybody else who thinks about meditation or has dabbled in meditation. Like, here we have this new body of research that is somewhat accepted but not universally accepted by the broad meditation community. So where did you land? Did you land on, I, Olga, will never go on a meditation retreat? I, Olga, will disdain my meditation teacher who tells me to just suck it up when I’m having sort of uncomfortable feelings? How did you integrate what you learned?

Khazan: Yeah. So Willoughby, where she kind of ended up, so she doesn’t meditate anymore, and—

Rosin: Oh.

Khazan: —she doesn’t teach at Brown, so she has kind of left it all behind. But that doesn’t mean that she herself is against meditation for everyone. And the rules that she gave me for how to meditate more safely or to minimize the risk of something bad happening are, I think, pretty simple and easy to follow and good.

So she basically says that meditating for more than 30 minutes a day is associated with generally more bad stuff. So people who meditate for less than 30 minutes a day, you don’t really start entering some of these states where you don’t really know who you are anymore or you see visions or things like that. You’re basically just gonna maybe get some of the upsides of meditation without delving into this dark side.

The other thing that she says is that if you are considering going on a meditation retreat, she doesn’t say don’t do it, but just try meditating in your house first. (Laughs.) Don’t go on one of these coming off of an 80-hour workweek, having never meditated, and try to make it through 10 days of silence.

The other thing she says is that different kinds of meditation can affect people differently. So people who are really anxious sometimes don’t do well with a body scan–type meditation, which is this type of meditation where you focus on different parts of your body very slowly one at a time. This didn’t bother me that much, even though I am very anxious. I kinda like the body scan. But some people have a really hard time with it.

[Music]

Khazan: And then she also says that it’s okay if you just wanna stop meditating. If it’s truly not for you and it’s not helping you and it’s making you feel worse, it’s okay to stop. I don’t know. I feel like we’re there with SSRIs. Like, if you’re on Prozac and it’s giving you a ton of side effects and you’re not feeling better, no doctor would be like, That’s part of how the Prozac works. Just keep pushing through it. But with meditation, for some reason, that hasn’t been the narrative around it. It’s more like If you don’t like it, you’re doing it wrong. And she really pushes back against that and says, If you don’t like it, maybe it’s not for you.

Khazan: Is there a particular mindfulness phrase that sets off alarm bells for you?

Britton: The only way forward is through.

Khazan: (Laughs.) Yeah.

Britton: It has to get worse before it gets better. What you resist persists. These are all sort of thought-terminating clichés. These are all ways of basically starting to undermine the ability to call something harm.

Rosin: Why do you think that Willoughby Britton completely stopped rather than adapting?

Khazan: I think there was just—she went too far, and then she had to go completely out. Hers was a true religious deconversion. And mostly people don’t deconvert from extreme zealot to slightly less extreme zealot. You know what I mean?

Rosin: Yeah.

Khazan: They usually just leave the religion entirely, which is literally what she did. I really think that she had a lot of hurt from the meditation community and their response to her research from her meditation experience itself from just this feeling of being the person who’s pointing out that meditation can be bad, which is, nobody wants to hear. I think there was just a lot of hurt that built up over time, and she just didn’t wanna do it anymore.

Rosin: Well, Olga, thank you so much for teaching us about this.

Khazan: Absolutely. Thanks for having me on.

Rosin: This is your dharma, Olga.

Khazan: This is my dharma. (Laughs.)

Rosin: Yeah, exactly.

Khazan: Namaste, y’all.

[Music]

Rosin: This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Jinae West with help from Jacob Smollen. It was edited by Kevin Townsend. Michelle Ciarrocca fact-checked. Rob Smierciak engineered and provided original music. We also had music from Breakmaster Cylinder. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of Atlantic audio, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor.

Listeners, if you enjoy the show, you can support our work and the work of all Atlantic journalists when you subscribe to The Atlantic at TheAtlantic.com/Listener.

I’m Hanna Rosin. Thank you for listening.

entries.title: College Is Coming Apart
entries.summary: Successive, overlapping crises reveal that American higher education makes no sense.
entries.content:
Successive, overlapping crises reveal that American higher education makes no sense.

Sign up for Ordinary Extraordinary, Ian Bogost’s newsletter on making everyday life vivid.

Artificial intelligence arrived on campus as a crisis but has since become banal. Students can now do basically all their schoolwork automatically with AI—answering scientific problem sets, writing computer code, and drafting essays. Professors like me have no idea whether we are really teaching or just LARPing for students who are also pretending to occupy their role. Worse, some of us are offloading the drudgery of writing recommendation letters, grant proposals, and even scientific papers to AI.

But at the same time that AI fouled up the student-teacher relationship, the technology benefited other corners of campus. Researchers quickly discovered that AI is enormously useful for knowledge production, especially in the natural and applied sciences: in protein-structure prediction, materials design, and drug discovery, for example. Pressured, in part, by donors, boards, employers, and parents, college administrators have announced AI initiatives, invested in AI infrastructure, and established AI degree programs.

These two forces—students using AI to their detriment and colleges using it to their benefit—might seem to be in conflict. Students are supposed to do everything longhand to preserve the sanctity of learning, but they are also urged to meet the new professional demands created by AI. Faculty and administrators are policing the classroom for AI, largely in vain, while also using AI liberally in their own work. Campuses are defending themselves against AI as an interloper while concurrently retooling themselves for the AI future. Colleges are racing toward and away from AI simultaneously. It feels like artificial intelligence is wresting higher education apart.

That’s what I thought at first too. But I’ve come to the conclusion that something bigger, stranger, and more damaging has been taking place for a long time. AI has combined with two other recent campus crises—the coronavirus pandemic and the research-funding cuts of the second Trump administration—to amplify a deeper truth: American college is incompatible with itself. Americans speak of “college” as if it is one coherent thing. That’s wrong. Higher education is a bundle of unrelated things held together by custom, history, and accident. The college bundle was always a tenuous one. It has little reason to remain together, even as the institutions inside it are too entrenched to separate.

College in America makes two promises. On the one hand, college is a credentialing service: It awards a degree that affirms knowledge and sends a graduate into a career. On the other hand, college is a coming-of-age service. It forms identity through social exploration and intellectual development. It is the American ideal for how a young person figures out who they are. Partying, drinking, Greek life, sports, and other forms of college life always risked undermining the educational project—and vice versa. But the two categories coexisted well enough.

Now two things that got packaged together as “college” have begun to unbundle and disperse. The coming-of-age experience—friendships, independence, experimentation—has become less obviously dependent on the campus surrounding it, partly because college’s monopoly on exposure to a wider world weakened. Globalization and the internet bring much of that world to students long before they arrive on campus. Other aspects of college life have been moving off campus too. College football has gone national, abandoning regional affinities and local rivalries. Greek rush has become an outsourced industry. Campuses are hospital systems, major local employers, and real-estate-investment operations as much as, or more than, they are schools.

Optimizing college for professional preparation also began to pull the two purposes apart, and eroded the unrepeatable social experience that college is supposed to provide. The economy demanded more of students outside the classroom—internships, networking, publications, volunteering. In a brutal job-search environment, where entry-level gigs seem to demand nepotism, luck, and 10 rounds of interviews, today’s undergraduates may feel that their older professors do not fully understand the gap between the delivery of the credential and the career it promises.

Then COVID-19 revealed that the credentialing process could continue if campus life was reduced or even eliminated entirely. Considerable controversy and confusion accompanied this moment; some students tried to sue expensive universities on the grounds that a closed campus was not worth the full-freight price. But in the end, credentialing proved entirely possible with a compromised or absent version of campus life.

Now AI has separated the two purposes of college almost entirely. Writing an essay previously required doing something resembling the assigned academic work. Because AI makes it possible to complete coursework without much or any intellectual labor, AI has disconnected the output from the process (if students choose the shortcut). Suffering through a term paper no longer inherently affords opportunities to take a break to get a late-night coffee with your fellow students, to commiserate with hallmates over a difficult professor, or to reach an unexpected realization while drunk at a house party. Social and academic progress are no longer woven together. No particular quantity of shared time or deliberation is required to carry out one inside the other.

A combination of factors (among them shifting values, educational entrepreneurship, regulatory arbitrage, and the speed of technological change) has altered the meaning of a diploma. Yet schools have had no trouble continuing to award degrees to the students who spent their whole undergraduate careers on campuses that tout the same traditional look on quads and inside libraries, but that AI has hopelessly mangled beneath the surface.

Immediately after taking office, the second Trump administration embarked on a series of attacks against higher education. The attacks were politically motivated, but they were effective because they hit campuses where it hurt. Since World War II, the American research-university sector has become defined as an enormous, distributed, scientific-research industry. The Trump attacks undermined this project by disrupting the tens of billions of dollars of federal funding that pays for that research (which includes graduate education).

At the same moment that AI was widening the conflict between credentialing and coming of age, the Trump cuts exposed a different structural incompatibility, between education and research. The fact that big universities were driven by research was not a secret, but it was also not well understood by the American public, including parents and students. If you find out that a friend or neighbor is a university professor, you’d probably ask them, “What do you teach?” And if they squirm when asked, that’s because many faculty often do not see teaching as their primary job. Yes, a professor is expected to teach undergraduates and produce research, because a university’s mission entails education and scholarship. But national universities do not value or reward those activities equally.

Research brings grants, prestige, graduate students, rankings, and career advancement. At research universities, undergraduate teaching is seen, if not described, as a necessary act to keep the tuition dollars flowing and to maintain the appearance of undergraduate education as predominant—the thing that people think of first when they imagine what college is for.

University administrators often argue that the research and teaching missions bolster each other: A star researcher, the story goes, can bring the latest knowledge to the classroom. Basically every college tour on an American campus will include a schtick about how undergraduates can participate in faculty research. Universities have a strong incentive to make research and teaching appear to align. But in truth, those purposes sit more in tension than in unity.

A revealing term helps explain how tenuous this relationship really is. A researcher who gets a big grant can use part of those funds for a “teaching buyout,” paying their way out of the classroom. Success at one of the university’s missions literally purchases relief from the other. (There is no research buyout.)

Campuses such as mine, Washington University in St. Louis, take in $1 billion or more of research funding every year. That money pays for the work done in labs, but also for equipment, buildings, and staff. It forms the foundation for the metrics (grants won, and “research expenditures,” or money spent from those grants) that campuses use to compete against one another for faculty, graduate students, philanthropic gifts, and other forms of prestige. Threaten the flow of research money and you don’t merely endanger the labs; you destabilize the financial and organizational structure of the whole sector.

Every major college and university touts the liberal arts as the core of an undergraduate education, but the humanities in particular—fields of arts and letters such as literature and languages, which generally do not receive much, if any, federal research funding—enjoy mostly vestigial value that does not match the underlying economics of higher education very well. Universities are different from colleges in this regard. Small liberal-arts colleges focus almost exclusively on undergraduate education and are earnestly committed to the arts and letters. That’s one reason they are particularly well positioned to weather the Trump attacks. But these schools serve much smaller populations, and they are still tied to the broader American university system, from which they draw faculty and to which they send students on to grad school. And even at these schools, the humanities are particularly vulnerable to AI, because the intellectual labor that the technology can now eliminate—wrestling with the meaning of texts, figuring out how to express complex ideas—is the fundamental point of that type of education.

The AI crisis on campus, mated to the COVID-19 and federal-funding crises that flanked it, dismantled the pretense that everything happening on campus shared any kind of common project. AI might substantially improve scientific research while destroying the humanities. And AI might troublingly reduce the effort a student must exert to complete a degree while allowing a scientist to carry out experiments with reduced labor, uncontroversially.

Undergraduate education, credentialing, scientific research, professionalization, and coming of age still occupy the same campuses. But they are clearly no longer parts of the same enterprise. They have not been so for many years—probably many decades. Looking back at my own career, I can see clearly that every single term of it has taken place in the shadow of this family of mismatches. Teaching and research sometimes align, but not always. Becoming educated has little to do with becoming an adult, apart from taking place on the same campus. I used to understand a university as akin to a city—expansive, diverse, and necessarily host to multiple purposes. But now I wonder if even that generous account is a fantasy. I wonder if one organization can support all of these conflicting projects well—and if it ever did.

Now that these incompatibilities are harder to ignore, will the American collegiate project reinvent itself in a way that would resolve them? Perhaps, but also: I doubt it. Universities are purpose-built to resist change of almost any kind. College leaders have repeatedly adopted a “wait and see” or “keep our heads down” approach, treating disruption as mere interruption: The pandemic ended, AI will settle down, federal funding will resume, and all of this, whatever it is, will blow over. These are far more tolerable conclusions to reach than, say, the idea that credentialing has no business sharing a venue with coming of age, or that undergraduate education is at odds with the mission of a research institution.

Each recent crisis gave college an alibi. AI was an alien technology that corrupted an otherwise functional educational institution. The Trump funding cuts were an aberrant political attack on a healthy research enterprise. COVID-19 was an emergency that forced campuses to suspend campus life and education alike in the interest of public health. But surviving any one of these crises, let alone all of them together, changes nothing about the underlying circumstances that they exacerbated. The incompatible purposes of college carry on.

I see no reason to believe that the structural inconsistencies that have come to define higher education will resolve. The degree will become ever more a goal and less a process of self-discovery. The research and teaching missions will further retract from each other. College is at war with itself as much as it is with the public, or the government, or the private sector, or the technology industry.

As a degree or a ritual, college will continue to have value, and you or your kids may want to attend one for a credential or a coming-of-age experience (or both). The old names will persist, and the campus buildings will still stand. The coursework will continue whether humans or machines complete it (or assign it). The leaves will fall onto the quad in the autumn, and the caps will fly into the air in the spring. The appearance of college can endure, even as its spirit—a community organized for the education and formation of young people—comes undone.

entries.title: Why the Bomb Is Bad for Democracy
entries.summary: A famous documentarian’s new book suggests that secrecy is a major impediment to sensible nuclear policy.
entries.content:
A famous documentarian’s new book suggests that secrecy is a major impediment to sensible nuclear policy.

“In August of 1945, the city of Hiroshima was destroyed in about nine seconds by a single atomic bomb.” So begins the 1981 documentary The Day After Trinity, in a voice-over against a black background. “The man responsible for building the bomb was a gentle and eloquent physicist named J. Robert Oppenheimer.”

Directed by a young filmmaker named Jon Else and financed by a public-television station in San Jose, The Day After Trinity quickly became a hit across the United States. One of its innovations was to pair the story of the bomb with that of Oppenheimer, foregrounding the contradiction of this “gentle” pacifist giving the nation its greatest weapon of war. As the historian David K. Hecht has argued, Else’s film helped transform Oppenheimer from a Cold War political figure into a symbol of the profound moral dilemmas inherent in the nuclear age.

In the years since the documentary premiered, Americans have continued to view Oppenheimer (and, by extension, his bomb) through Else’s lens. American Prometheus, the Pulitzer Prize–winning biography written by Kai Bird and Martin J. Sherwin, repeatedly cites Else’s interview transcripts and largely replicates his approach. Oppenheimer, Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster 2023 film adaption of the book, does much the same.

Now Else, at 82, has revisited the bomb, this time in a nonfiction book he’s been working on for 20 years. Yet Frenchman Flat: The Rise and Fall of Atomic Bombs is not another story of the doomed Oppenheimer; Else relies on his own remarkable interviews from almost half a century ago but doesn’t focus on the scientist, and he declines to “relitigate the decision to drop the bomb” on Japan.

Neither is Frenchman Flat quite what its publisher is promoting, the “story of a single nuclear bomb” (a 37-kiloton nuke called Priscilla that exploded over Frenchman Flat, a dry lake bed in Nevada, in 1957). That story, though compellingly told, disappears for whole swaths of the text. Instead, much to its credit, the book unspools an unhurried, capacious story of human society’s collective journey to the brink of annihilation, and of the individuals and movements that have, so far, held us back from the edge. It is a major work, highlighting the heroism and the absurdity of our atomic present and this Strangelovian, Lovecraftian thing we call “nuclear policy.”

Today, the famous Doomsday Clock, which measures the risk of nuclear cataclysm, is at just 85 seconds from midnight, the closest it’s been to Armageddon since the clock’s creation in 1947. After decades of disarmament, Russia, China, France, and several other nuclear powers are rapidly expanding their arsenals, while Germany, South Korea, Japan, and others are considering developing their own programs. The agreements that long ago halted U.S. and Russian testing recently expired. Donald Trump has been expressing an alarming interest in the use of nuclear weapons for decades.

Among Else’s most important accomplishments is recognizing how crucial secrecy has been to the maintenance of nuclear stockpiles. Since the bomb was first developed, the U.S. government has denied the public basic facts about atomic weapons. “The extreme secrecy surrounding almost everything concerning nuclear weapons impeded effective democratic debate for decades,” one report quoted by Else concluded. The bomb, in other words, is bad for democracy, just as democracy is bad for the bomb.

The tight grip on information goes back to the beginning—to the Manhattan Project, which brought hundreds of scientists and their families to the New Mexico desert to build an unprecedented weapon. At the height of World War II, the U.S. military concluded that the decision to develop a bomb could not be subject to public debate. Even among members of the U.S. Congress, the historian Alex Hellerstein has calculated, only about 1 percent were brought into the loop. In 1943, the wartime Office of Censorship banned media references to “war experiments,” and officials issued false or misleading responses to press inquiries. Thus, when a bomb exploded onto Hiroshima and “instantly broiled the skin of every person in the open within half a mile,” in Else’s appropriately gruesome phrasing, almost everyone on the planet was genuinely shocked.

But that was wartime—and the cessation of hostilities generated new complexities. Could this degree of unaccountability really persist in a time of peace? Else’s interview subjects felt that it shouldn’t. Within weeks of Japan’s surrender, hundreds of Manhattan Project scientists put out a statement calling for “free and enlightened public discussion” of atomic power. Oppenheimer and liberal members of Harry S. Truman’s administration quickly proposed a plan to place control of all nuclear materials and weapons in the hands of the United Nations.

As the historian Daniel Immerwahr has noted, much of the scientific community went so far as to seek a “global government” to regulate the bomb. Today this idea might seem unthinkable, but in the ’40s, the notion enjoyed the support of such wild-eyed radicals as Winston Churchill, Richard Nixon, John F. Kennedy, and Ronald Reagan. The postwar constitutions of France and Italy explicitly countenanced a future global body that would trump their own sovereignty. Else cites polls suggesting that about two-thirds of Americans supported some version of this concept.

It did not come to pass. U.S. leaders waffled on the idea, and eventually the U.S.S.R., hastily developing a bomb of its own, rejected it. What, then, to do with America’s swelling nuclear arsenal? Many elected officials feared that some “dashing lieutenant colonel” might go rogue with a nuke or three, and so in 1946, Congress passed the Atomic Energy Act, taking control of the bomb away from the military and placing it solely in the hands of the president.

Given the trigger-happy proposals floated by many within the military brass in the years to follow, this structure may well have saved countless lives, but it hardly provided for democratic accountability, much less actual arms control. The historian Garry Wills has powerfully argued that the postwar nuclear chain of command altered the United States “down to its deepest constitutional roots,” giving the president exclusive and unfettered power far beyond the comprehension of our country’s founders. Kennedy, for one, considered the presidential nuclear prerogative “insane.”

Much of Frenchman Flat is devoted to documenting the insanity that resulted from a nuclear-powered state (and, soon, states) freed from checks and balances and uninterested in public debate. There was no public hearing concerning the U.S. decision to start exploding nuclear bombs in Nevada in 1951; the state’s governor heard about it only a week before the first bomb fell. For years thereafter, the government insisted that nuclear fallout was safe, even as kids across the desert West started receiving leukemia diagnoses. Decades later, studies estimated that as many as 212,000 cases of cancer resulted from U.S. nuclear testing.

Meanwhile, behind closed doors, the global superpowers were accelerating the arms race. Both the Americans and the Soviets seriously considered nuclear testing on the moon. The first U.S. test of a hydrogen bomb (hundreds to thousands of times stronger than an atom bomb) was in 1952, and the first Soviet H-bomb test followed in 1953. When a government committee chaired by Oppenheimer recommended strongly against the development of the H-bomb, the Atomic Energy Commission buried the report by classifying it as secret. The H-bomb’s existence became public only after a congressman inadvertently disclosed it on live television. Even Truman hadn’t learned of the “super bomb” until years after its development began.

Over the course of the 1950s, as information leaked, public opposition to nuclear testing spread. Impelled by increasing discontent, the Americans and Soviets tentatively entered arms-control discussions. In 1963, they agreed to halt aboveground nuclear testing (underground testing would cease 30 years later). Dozens of countries suspended in-progress nuclear programs. “We are alive to discuss these things thanks in large measure to the grand patchwork of treaties, agreements, and unilateral actions,” Else writes.

Yet the nuclear peace has always been a fragile one. At least twice, full-scale nuclear war has likely been averted only because a single individual—Vasily Arkhipov in 1962 and Stanislav Petrov in 1983—decided to stand in the way. The U.S. and Russia still have about 5,000 bombs apiece, more than enough to end human civilization. Only voluntary forbearance precludes renewed testing or development or, for that matter, the deployment of intercontinental ballistic missiles and B-2 stealth bombers that are always at the ready. The oceans still teem with nuclear submarines, Else notes, “each boat packing more firepower than what was spent in all the wars in history.” The “nuclear club,” according to an essay in this magazine, is on track to double.

Remarkably, Else concludes Frenchman Flat on a note of ambivalence about this unstable status quo. “I have come to appreciate deterrence and understand that until we learn differently our bombs may save us from their bombs,” Else writes. Global abolition, the goal of generations of peace activists, including Martin Luther King Jr. and Pope Leo XIV, is, he adds, “unrealistic.” He shares this perspective with several of his interview subjects, who are international negotiators—members in good standing of what Else labels the “diplomatic bomb squad.” At the same time, he recognizes the absurdity of the nuclear buildup. “Why are you so concerned with saving lives?” he quotes one U.S. general as having said in 1963. “Look, at the end of the war, if there are two Americans and one Russian, we win.”

Ultimately, Else does not recommend a path out of the nuclear quagmire (which in fairness was not the task he set for himself). In any event, our international institutions are presently far too weak to provide the supranational control envisioned by mid-century luminaries, and a good number of our current world leaders are almost uniquely ill-suited to steer political bodies that are armed to the teeth.

Yet Frenchman Flat does provide some directional cues toward a safer future. Integral to an awareness of nuclear dangers is an end to the regime of secrecy—or at least substantial reform. Democratic oversight of this greatest weapon of war is impossible if the people are deprived of basic information. Of course, democracy is not a sufficient condition for disarmament, much less abolition. The H-bomb was popular with the American public at moments of peak anti-Soviet fervor, just as 70 percent of South Koreans, facing a nuclear regime to the north, want the bomb today. Nonetheless, popular discontent, often driven by leaked information, has historically curbed the nuclear ambitions of many of the most martial leaders. It is reasonable to imagine that even more awareness would spur even more opposition.

Sunlight alone will not solve the problem of nuclear proliferation. The aim of the abolitionists, realistic or not, has always been not just to eliminate the bombs but also to alter the conditions that might lead countries to use them. The prospect of a future free of mushroom clouds, they believe, is inseparable from a global order built on cooperation and democracy.
