entries.title: Who Made America Poorer and Dirtier?
entries.summary: The people in charge are really hoping you’ll blame someone else.
entries.content:
The people in charge are really hoping you’ll blame someone else.

At last week’s GOP midterm convention in Dallas, Vice President Vance painted a bleak picture of American life before the second Trump administration:

“Two years ago, we have to remember, our nation, ladies and gentlemen, was tired. We were tired of seeing our factories close. We were tired of our neighbors dying of drug overdoses. We were tired of not being able to afford anything. We were tired of seeing the cartels and the criminals given free rein over our great country,” Vance said. “And we were tired of being called racist for noticing that our country was becoming dirtier and poorer and less safe and less prosperous.”

Who is responsible for this terrible state of affairs? The opposition party and immigrants, apparently. Vance went on to say, “The Democrat legacy of the last few years was that they bankrupted our country and left us poor. They left our country weaker. They left our border wide open and our communities less safe.”

But this account represents a preposterous inversion. Almost every problem Vance lists, the Trump administration has made worse.

The administration’s environmental policies have made American water and air dirtier. Its health-care, tariff, and tax policies have worsened inflation and increased the financial burden on most American households, even as incomes have grown. And its public-health policies have led to outbreaks of contagious disease.

The Environmental Protection Agency under President Trump has revoked regulations on air pollution—including those on particulate matter that can cause heart and lung disease—after being intensely lobbied by the fossil-fuel industry. It has repealed limits on “forever chemicals” in drinking water, which are linked to cancer and other health problems. The Trump Justice Department scrapped a settlement compelling Alabama to provide adequate sanitation systems to residents living with raw sewage, describing it as “DEI.” After the residents of Jackson, Mississippi, learned they had been drinking lead-tainted tap water, a Trump-appointed federal judge ruled that Americans don’t have a constitutional right to clean drinking water.

Although Trump won the 2024 election largely because of Biden-era inflation, he has done everything in his power to make inflation worse. Trump’s arguably illegal and certainly ill-advised war in Iran has led to the closure of strategic shipping waterways, which has provoked a rise in energy prices, which has in turn raised the prices of other goods. Trump’s tariffs worsened inflation by raising the price of imports, and wages seem to be falling behind inflation. To make matters worse, health-care costs are rising rapidly, in part because of the Trump administration’s repeal of Affordable Care Act subsidies in its One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

Crime is down. But that’s not because of the Trump administration’s mass-deportation program, whose brutal and indiscriminate tactics have weakened the economy rather than strengthened it. The reality is that immigrants are far less likely than native-born Americans to commit crimes, and crime has been falling steadily since the pandemic-induced spike in 2020 and 2021. Absent significant changes to the space-time continuum, Trump cannot claim credit for a decline in crime that began before Trump even took office, especially with an FBI director who devotes bureau resources to respond to people mocking him on X.

Vance called out two women, one of whom was born in Somalia, who defrauded Medicaid of $46 million. But the Trump administration has been happy to pardon fraudsters such as Lawrence Duran, who was sentenced to 50 years in prison for defrauding Medicare of more than $200 million, or Robert Harshbarger Jr., the husband of Republican Representative Diana Harshbarger, who pleaded guilty to health-care fraud. Last February, Elizabeth Oyer, a former U.S. pardon attorney, told The New York Times that Trump’s pardons had “essentially wiped away about $1 billion in penalties and restitution secured by federal prosecutors in fraud cases.” But the number may be even larger; Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee estimated in August that the number is closer to $2 billion.

Safety isn’t just about crime, and in this respect, the Trump administration has tried its best to make the federal government worse at protecting Americans from foreseeable problems. Cuts to public agencies have coincided with outbreaks of infectious and foodborne diseases, to the point that the administration is trying to manipulate numbers to hide measles deaths. I don’t know about you, but I felt safer when I could eat lettuce without thinking about whether it would make me sick. Or berries. Or beef.

In fairness, however, not everyone is getting poorer—the top 1 and 0.1 percent of American households have seen their income grow considerably, thanks to the OBBBA’s slashing of taxes on the wealthy; the bottom 50 percent, not so much. This is a trend that began long before Trump—and has been sustained in part by the Democrats’ unwillingness to reverse Republicans’ tax cuts. To the extent that anyone should be happy with the Trump administration’s policies, though, many of its extremely wealthy backers are getting all they paid for and then some.

As for everyone else? The country is almost certainly dirtier, poorer, less prosperous, and in some ways less safe than in 2024. But that’s not because of Democrats or immigrants. It’s because of the people currently running the place. They’re really hoping you’ll blame someone else.

entries.title: The Dead Silence of AI Therapy
entries.summary: What happens when our therapists are no longer able to feel?
entries.content:
What happens when our therapists are no longer able to feel?

Therapy can involve a lot of words, but it’s often the pauses that matter most. If you transcribed a session, the pauses would look like nothing: beats of silence, extra breaths, slowing down. But these can represent the crux of the practice: entry points into feeling. My job as a psychoanalyst is to listen as much to silence as to words, to be present with the patient while they’re quiet—to stay with them as they allow their feelings to emerge.

I was trained across diverse theories and techniques, but in my clinical work I have found that the cornerstone of the process is feeling. The patient’s emotional experience is the destination and the terrain. But I also feel; I am moved. And the work I do with my patients relies on our relationship and our capacity for mutual feeling. In many ways, the history of my field from Freud on has been a growing acknowledgement of the reality of this relationship—moving from the therapist as sealed off and standing apart, toward approaches that view the real human relationship between patient and therapist as the territory where healing happens.

Now the rise of the AI therapist is upon us. The growing cadre of AI mental-health services tend to avoid using words like therapist and therapy. They say that they do not replace professional help and that they can refer users to human therapists if needed. But their positioning as a therapy-like service is clear. In June, the therapy giant Talkspace launched its AI mental-health agent, Tee, “developed to help individuals navigate life’s daily mental health challenges.” Then there’s Ash, which offers to support your “emotional wellbeing,” helping you to “connect the dots between thoughts, feelings, and behaviors.” Abby promises to be “warm, thoughtful, and direct” and to help you “work through the kinds of everyday emotional challenges that often go unspoken.” And Headspace’s Ebb advertises: “Stressed at work? Family drama? Trouble sleeping? Ebb can help you unpack what’s on your mind and move forward with more clarity.”

When I reached Talkspace for comment, a company spokesperson told me in an email that Tee is “absolutely not a replacement for human therapy. It is a safe AI mental-health guide that can be used to talk through situations like stress, anxiety, relationships, life challenges, and personal growth.”

AI therapy is a radical move, and we need to reckon with what happens when we turn to therapists who cannot feel.

Therapy and AI have been intertwined since the technology’s beginnings. One of the first chatbots, Eliza, built at MIT in the mid-1960s, ran a therapy script called DOCTOR that asked users questions about their feelings and experiences—and left its creator disconcerted about his technology’s strong emotional pull. Since chatbots such as ChatGPT and Claude have burst onto the scene, large swaths of the population have been using non-therapy-branded AIs for emotional and mental-health support. Two cultural forces are coming together right now: the growing embrace and destigmatization of therapy, and the idea, explicitly espoused by Silicon Valley, that AI can accomplish what patients seek. I was interested to see how these tools worked in practice, so, although I could not be a neutral observer, I signed up for Tee and attended a few sessions.

After I logged in, the chatbot moved me through predetermined session stages that I could follow on my screen’s right-hand corner: Agenda Setting, Active Conversation, Core Work, Practice Plan, Session Complete. It encouraged me to talk about whatever I wanted to, but in the beginning focused on identifying a clear-cut problem, which it wanted to set as the session’s “agenda.” With the agenda set, we went back and forth a bit until the bot suggested that we “shift now from exploring the problem to building a small, realistic step forward.” Its proposed remedy was an exercise patterned on cognitive behavioral therapy that involved pausing for 90 seconds each day before I started work. These sorts of exercises can be helpful. But, in this cycle of identifying problems and fixes, we did not touch what is underneath.

The chatbot was also willing to “just talk it through,” rather than offering a concrete suggestion. When we took this route, I could tell that the bot was attempting active listening—restating and asking questions about my experience, mimicking empathy. That’s a process that can help clarify thoughts, but knowing that no one was behind the dialogue, that the empathy was a technique and not a presence, left me with a sense of being poignantly unheard.

Much of what matters in therapy happens in nonverbal communication. During a recent session, a patient of mine spoke flatly about upcoming social plans. Then he stopped momentarily, and his eyes softened and drifted downward. The silence that opened felt profound. After a time, I said, “I wonder what happened just there.” He took a breath and began moving into emotional territory that he had long kept out of view.

Tee, meanwhile, had a different approach to silence.

First, I told the chatbot about my week and how I’d been doing. It validated my emotions (“that makes sense”), asked for more detail, and around we went. But whenever I stopped typing, and might have dipped into the more meaningful recesses of myself, the chatbot in front of me was inert and lifeless. The nonverbal interplay between selves that is so important in human therapy was palpably absent. Being silent with the chatbot did not feel like an invitation to being together, but rather like a kind of deadness. I felt the strong impulse to type quickly to spur the machine back to life. There was no indication that the bot remained with me as I quietly began to feel.

It is true that AI can simulate presence and empathy—sometimes fairly convincingly. That’s why people adopt chatbots as confidants and therapists in the first place. And it’s likely that future versions of the therapy bots will get better at making silence feel more meaningful. But there is a wide gulf between AI conveying I understand you and I am here with you, and AI actually being with you. Mimicking presence feels more like emotional deception. When patients trust their therapist and the therapy process, they move into a vulnerable place—and being deceived this way leads to ineffective therapy at best, and may cause harm.

Most critiques of AI therapy focus on AI’s sycophancy—its failure to intervene and challenge destructive patterns of thought and action, contributing to suicides, manic episodes, and psychotic states. These critiques, while important, carry forward the old model of the therapist as a dispassionate technician. They see AI therapy as harmful because it does not act upon the patient correctly. This is a framework that the technology companies can get behind. They respond that, sure, the current chatbots have problems, but these are fixable. OpenAI and other companies have taken to publishing statistics demonstrating that their chatbots are making gains in terms of intervening with distressed users in appropriate ways. The underlying argument is that mental-health support is a set of techniques and interventions, and that once machines learn to marshal these effectively, all will be well.

In my work with patients, I keep theories and techniques in mind, but the most important element of the process is striving to be fully present. If there is a North Star in this work, it is being with patients in their emotional experience in a deep and lasting way.

This approach is borne out in the rich psychoanalytic literature on empathy and emotional dwelling. Trauma is most enduring when patients have felt alone in it, and one of the best pathways toward healing is coming to feel that another person remains with you in your suffering, and thus that you are no longer alone. And studies on what helps patients in therapy, across different therapeutic modalities, illustrate the importance of the human relationship and of the patient and therapist being able to express emotion.

AI is an alluring alternative to traditional therapy. The barriers to entry are almost nonexistent: Gone are the friction and labor of finding a human therapist, building trust, and opening up. And AI’s promise of affordable therapy is genuinely appealing. The economics of human therapy are broken. The U.S. in particular is in profound need of insurance reform and legislation that will make therapy affordable for all. In this field as in all fields, AI is not going back into the bottle, and I imagine that it may take on useful adjunct roles in mental-health care.

But AI therapy cannot meet our needs. Whatever inroads people take into AI therapy, the strongest pull, if not on the surface then as a current beneath, will be the yearning for someone who can feel with you as you move further into yourself. At the heart of AI therapy is a paradox: We embrace it out of our longing for exactly what it cannot ultimately give.

entries.title: A Plan to Pay Married Mothers Not to Work
entries.summary: And make single moms pay for it.
entries.content:
The parents of young kids don’t have it easy in the United States. The country doesn’t have mandatory paid parental leave. It does not send out a child allowance. It doesn’t offer universal prekindergarten or provide day-care subsidies to all families in need. For the first five years of their kid’s life, parents are mostly left to figure it out on their own, negotiating a complex patchwork of federal, state, and local initiatives and spending far more than they can afford on diapers, formula, nanny shares, and the like.

These policies—or the lack of them—have harmed long-range educational and employment outcomes, eroded public health, entrenched inequality, discouraged couples from having children, and stressed the bejesus out of parents. For this crisis, Vice President Vance has a solution: send cash to married parents who stay at home with their kids.

According to a report by The New York Times, the White House has drafted a plan to allow nonworking married parents to collect payments from the federal Child Care and Development Fund. It will not surprise you to learn that I, the author of a book called Give People Money, think that providing cash to families taking care of their kids at home isn’t a bad idea at all. Yet given how rickety and stingy the country’s system of early-childhood support already is, the specifics of Vance’s proposal could produce astonishingly cruel results. That’s because he proposes to fund this new benefit by taking financial resources away from working single parents.

Currently, Washington distributes a $12 billion pot of CCDF money to the states each year. Governments use the cash to subsidize the cost of day care for low-income parents who are working, enrolled in school, or attending a training program. The typical beneficiary receives $700 a month, in the form of a voucher or a direct payment to their child-care provider. Four in five recipients are single mothers, many living on poverty wages. If the White House makes the changes under consideration—which Congress would not have to approve—low-income married couples with a stay-at-home parent could apply for cash transfers from the CCDF too. The $12 billion pot, however, would not get any bigger.

The proposal is a priority for Vance, who has championed policies to pay parents instead of child-care centers for years. Such initiatives would support women who want to care for their babies and toddlers, rather than encouraging them to work and thus imposing “the values of an increasingly isolated American ruling class” on the public, he wrote in a 2021 op-ed co-authored with Jenet Erickson of Brigham Young University. These initiatives would “mean happier parents and healthier children,” they argued, citing studies showing that kids in day care have worse social outcomes than kids cared for at home.

By paying women to remain out of the labor force, the White House’s proposal would indeed nudge parents away from day care. It would also deprive low-income single parents of financial support, and encourage married couples to earn less. As Patrick T. Brown of the Ethics and Public Policy Center has observed, a married couple in Kentucky with two kids might get a large transfer if they earn $81,500 a year, and zilch if they make a few hundred dollars more. Meanwhile, the country’s broader system of early-childhood support would remain broken, leaving babies and toddlers at risk.

The most obvious issue with Vance’s proposal comes down to simple math. The White House is not expanding the CCDF budget so that states can provide benefits to stay-at-home and working parents. Rather, it is making millions of additional people eligible for a capped pool of money, far too small to meet demand as is. In any given month, five out of every six families who qualify for subsidies do not receive them, according to the Department of Health and Human Services. Some families don’t know they exist or don’t bother applying. Some desperately need the help, but get put on a waitlist or denied aid. If the White House has its way, states will redirect some of this money from single parents to married couples. But the former generally have lower incomes than the latter. Even when a single parent makes as much as a married couple do, they typically have a tighter budget because they can’t rely on a partner for child care.

Vance and other conservatives have suggested that the policy would encourage unwed parents to get hitched, which they believe would reduce the poverty rate and promote children’s well-being in the long term. Individuals who follow the “success sequence”—get an education, get a job, get married, then have a kid—tend to make it to the middle class and stay there, after all. Yet many government policies discourage low-income parents from marrying by reducing the value of credits and transfers when couples file a single 1040. Some evidence suggests that eliminating so-called marriage penalties would boost the marriage rate. No evidence suggests that altering eligibility for an arcane, non-guaranteed child-care benefit would do so. The White House would just be steering cash to couples who had already made it to the altar.

As for those single mothers: If they lose access to child-care subsidies, their day-to-day expenses would increase precipitously. They might have no choice but to drop out of the labor force. If they do, they might lose access to other forms of government support. That’s because Washington has spent the past 60 years tying financial aid to work. The earned-income tax credit and child tax credit scale up with earnings. Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, better known as welfare, requires mothers to be enrolled in school or have a job. Just last year, the Trump administration created or expanded work requirements for parents receiving Medicaid coverage and food stamps.

Vance has called the Medicaid policy “totally reasonable.” His memoir Hillbilly Elegy promulgates the notion that simple government transfers do not end poverty, and often make it worse. The book is an indictment of the Appalachian community that his extended family calls home: a “hub of misery” populated by do-nothing, take-everything welfare queens. But now he’s proposing a policy that seems to instantiate the idea that married, stay-at-home mothers cannot be welfare queens. Vance seems to believe that when a wife with no income takes cash from the government, she is raising her kids right—but that when an unmarried woman receives a child-care voucher from the government, she better be on the job, because she is sapping the public coffers.

This double standard has a clear racial valence: Two in three Black women who gave birth in 2024 were unmarried, versus one in four white women. Black kids are about three times as likely to be raised by a single mother as white kids are. Thus, the White House would not just be taking from highly financially vulnerable families to give to slightly less financially vulnerable families; it would be taking from Black families to give to white ones.

Remaining on the job might even get harder, given that the proposal would expand the country’s already formidable child-care deserts. Paying stay-at-home parents from this fixed pool of funds would deprive day-care centers of revenue. Some would offer fewer hours or hire less-qualified teachers. Some would close down. Working parents might end up having to enroll their toddlers in less convenient or lower-quality centers, or paying more for care.

The country’s parents need comprehensive reform, not this kind of regressive, zero-sum nanny-statism. They need Washington to amp up the child tax credit, mandate parental leave, eliminate marriage penalties, finance public preschool programs, and create universal-child-care subsidies. Pitting stay-at-home mothers against single mothers isn’t the answer.

entries.title: Kash Patel Refuses to Take a Republican’s Lifeline
entries.summary: The FBI director allowed a Senate hearing to turn into a discussion of bestiality.
entries.content:
The FBI director allowed a Senate hearing to turn into a discussion of bestiality.

This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.

President Trump appointed Kash Patel to lead the FBI not because of his brief experience in law enforcement but because he is a political brawler. The problem, as Patel demonstrated yesterday, is that he is not a very good one: No skilled political messenger would have allowed nearly every headline about a Senate hearing to connect their name and agency with bestiality.

Yesterday’s Senate Judiciary Committee hearing was Patel’s first appearance on Capitol Hill since a raucous visit in May. (At that hearing, Patel and Senator Chris Van Hollen verbally agreed to each take a self-screening test for alcohol abuse. Van Hollen posted his results the next day, but his office said it never heard back from Patel.) It was also Patel’s first hearing since CBS News revealed changes to FBI hiring standards, which reportedly now allow the bureau to consider applicants who have hired prostitutes fewer than three times, stole from an employer more than three years ago, or engaged in sex with animals before the age of 18.

Democrats were eager to press Patel on the changes, but the hearing’s buzziest exchange turned out to be between Patel and Senator John Kennedy of Louisiana, a Republican. During his questioning, Kennedy seemed to be doing everything he could to offer Patel a chance to defuse the story—but Patel, unable or unwilling to recognize the openings, didn’t take them.

The ranking Democrat, Senator Dick Durbin of Illinois, asked about the new requirements first. Patel said the bestiality change was designed to ensure that people who had been forced to engage in sex with animals were not shut out of an FBI job. “We did not want to punish victims of bestiality,” Patel said. “We are not going to target victims.” Whether this is accurate is unclear. The memo laying out the new standards has not been made public, but sources told CBS News that the rules “do not distinguish between candidates who were coerced into sexual activity with animals, as opposed to those who engaged in such acts willingly.”

Kennedy was the next senator to quiz Patel, and he tried to do some cleanup. “I’m really trying to understand,” he said, rubbing his face. “’Cause I listened to the exchange between you and Senator Durbin, and I’ve read a few news accounts, and I’m confused.” He asked Patel, almost rhetorically, to affirm that the FBI still had hiring standards, and Patel argued that changes had been necessary to ensure the quick hiring of good agents. As for bestiality, the old rule had “automatically disqualified any individual who participated on either side of it.”

Kennedy, a bit of a ham, couldn’t resist a jibe: “So you disqualified the animal?” But he was also losing patience. “I’m trying to understand why you did this,” he said, and then offered an unusually frank description of how many Senate hearings work today: “I understand the game. People try to make you look bad. We do the same thing when the other party’s in office.” He gave Patel another shot. The director replied that sometimes human traffickers force victims to engage in bestiality, and that the FBI did not want to disqualify victims—even though, again, the guidelines reportedly don’t make such a distinction.

An exasperated Kennedy wasn’t buying it. “Someone came to you and recommended” this? he asked. “And when you saw bestiality—I say this with respect—the person who recommended it, why didn’t you just say, ‘What planet did you parachute in from? Why do I wanna lead with my chin and get into bestiality?’”

One answer is that Patel just isn’t very politically astute. It’s hard to claim you’re cleaning up and reforming the FBI, as Patel has, when you’re allowing johns and people who stole from their employers to apply. As for bestiality, more careful wording of the FBI memo that first laid out the new standards would have avoided the controversy. Better preparation for the hearing might have given him a clearer explanation than what he offered. And sharper instincts would have told Patel that Kennedy was trying to help him out. Any high-level appointee should be able to get through a congressional hearing without bestiality becoming the main topic. Instead, Patel takes his cues from Trump, whose instinct is always to push back. But what works for Trump doesn’t work for others. It’s not even clear whether it works for Trump anymore.

Patel may have felt a need to loosen qualifications for agents because the FBI has experienced an exodus of staffers since he took over. More than 1,100 special agents, who had an average tenure of almost 22 years, left in 2025 alone, according to data from the Office of Personnel Management. Durbin has alleged that more than 5,000 nonpartisan civilian staffers departed last year. Some left of their own accord, and others were fired who were involved in investigations that Trump and Patel don’t like, such as those looking into the January 6 riot. This spring, my colleague Sarah Fitzpatrick reported that Patel’s colleagues had been concerned about what they described as Patel’s excessive drinking, repeated absences, emotional outbursts, and impulsive behavior. (Patel denied the allegations and sued Fitzpatrick and The Atlantic for defamation, demanding $250 million.)

If Patel doesn’t have the skills and temperament to run the FBI well, isn’t really cleaning up the bureau’s ranks, and can’t even get through a standard Senate hearing without things going off the rails, one might wonder why he’s in the job at all. Lower hiring standards apparently start at the top.

By Tony Frangie Mawad

Days after two deadly earthquakes struck northern Venezuela on June 24, killing at least 6,000 people and injuring tens of thousands more, the Venezuelan Seismological Research Foundation, known as Funvisis, made an unusual public plea: Could whoever had taken one of its GPS sensors please give it back?

For 13 years, the high-precision instrument had been bolted to a rocky outcrop in the hills of western Venezuela, quietly tracking the millimeter-scale movements of the Boconó fault, which was the likely source of the first of the two quakes. When Funvisis technicians went to recover the readings the sensor had stored, they found that the machine had gone missing. More than two months after the earthquakes, the organization still does not know who carried it off.

entries.title: What Nature’s Silence Said to Annie Dillard
entries.summary: The late writer believed that hearing the natural world is its own form of prayer.
entries.content:
The late writer believed that hearing the natural world is its own form of prayer.

“Nature’s silence is its one remark,” Annie Dillard wrote in a 1981 Atlantic essay. Dillard, who died yesterday at age 81, spent her life listening.

She opens that essay, “Teaching a Stone to Talk”—which was later adapted into a collection by the same title—with the story of a man named Larry who is trying to get a rock to speak to him. “He keeps it on a shelf,” she writes, protected “by a square of untanned leather, like a canary asleep under its cloth. Larry removes the cover for the stone’s lessons.” Dillard is not sure what exactly happens at these lessons, but she respects the process: “It is a noble work, and beats, from any angle, selling shoes.”

To Dillard, striving to hear the natural world was holy work too. “What have we been doing all these centuries but trying to call God back to the mountain, or, failing that, raise a peep out of anything that isn’t us?” she asks. Born in 1945 in Pittsburgh, she found inspiration in some of the places she lived. At age 28, she published Pilgrim at Tinker Creek, a Pulitzer Prize–winning nonfiction book that draws from her walks in the Blue Ridge Mountains in Virginia in the ’70s. Her musings on these solitary experiences in nature drew comparisons to Henry David Thoreau, who strongly influenced her work. She was also one of the first women to find a place in the male-dominated genre of wilderness writing. The writer Diana Saverin, who spent time going through an archive of Dillard’s personal writings and correspondence at Yale, once described in The Atlantic Dillard’s trepidation about how she would be received: “Before she published her book, she scribbled in her journal, wondering who would take her book seriously if its author was a ‘Virginia housewife named Annie.’”

She dealt with this problem by leaving her day-to-day suburban life out of her work, so much so that some critics felt that she was exaggerating just how often she was in the wildness of nature. As Saverin noted, Dillard acknowledged that “she sometimes distorted the literal truth to achieve an artistic one.” But to Dillard, the ultimate truths revealed themselves in the time she did spend outside. In her journals, she acknowledged the “theological” sensibility in her books, and it is there on every page. “What is the difference between a cathedral and a physics lab?” she wrote in The Atlantic. “Are they not both saying Hello” to the world beyond?

Throughout her life, Dillard identified, in turn, with Protestantism, Catholicism, and nothing at all. I first encountered her work in a religious-studies class at Wesleyan University, where she taught from 1979 to 2001, before my time there. Dillard was a shock to my system: Growing up as an observant but theologically confused Jew, I spent my teenage years in synagogue itchy with guilt, poring over the same words in the prayer book every Saturday and willing myself to believe. Only later did I come to understand that faith—and, perhaps more important, the very act of living—can also be found in what we see and touch and hear: even in the rustle of the wind. Dillard taught me this. “At a certain point you say to the woods, to the sea, to the mountains, the world, Now I am ready,” she wrote in 1981. “You feel the world’s word as a tension, a hum, a single chorused note everywhere the same. This is it: this hum is the silence. Nature does utter a peep—just this one.”

Sometimes nature thunders, giving us no choice but to listen. Describing a total eclipse, Dillard is in awe, even afraid: “It was as though an enormous, loping god in the sky had reached down and slapped the Earth’s face.” Other times, nature’s peep can feel anticlimactic, but this quiet commands reverence. The stone never does talk to Larry, and Dillard ends that story by succumbing to her faith in the nothingness. “You take a step in the right direction to pray to this silence,” she writes. “Pray without ceasing.”
